strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and timely question: whether language conditioning in pretrained text-to-image diffusion models can provide useful priors for monocular depth estimation. The proposed PriorDiffusion is a natural but relevant extension of diffusion-based depth estimators such as Marigold, and the problem motivation is compelling for controllable or user-guided 3D perception.

The evaluation covers several standard zero-shot depth benchmarks, including NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, and ScanNet, with comparisons to many established affine-invariant depth estimators. The reported results show consistent gains over the authors' reimplemented Marigold baseline, especially on KITTI and ETH3D, and improved convergence with fewer training iterations and fewer denoising steps.

The paper includes useful ablations beyond aggregate benchmark tables: prompt variants, blank/template text inputs, denoising-step sweeps, small-region evaluation using segmentation masks, and failure cases with incorrect language. These experiments help characterize when language helps and where it can mislead the model.

Qualitative examples are well aligned with the central hypothesis: captions can highlight small, low-contrast, partially occluded, or otherwise easily missed objects, and the visualizations suggest plausible improvements in these regions.
weaknesses: The main empirical gains over the strongest directly comparable baseline are modest. In Table 1, PriorDiffusion improves over the reimplemented Marigold by about 0.1-0.6 δ1 points and 0.2-0.4 AbsRel points on most benchmarks, and it does not outperform large-scale depth foundation models such as Depth Anything/Depth Anything v2 on several datasets. Therefore, the repeated state-of-the-art framing is overstated unless restricted to similarly trained diffusion models or methods using fewer than 100K training images.

The causal evidence that the gains come from meaningful language priors is not fully convincing. Table 5 shows that blank or generic template prompts already recover much of the performance, suggesting that part of the improvement may come from architecture/training differences, regularization, or use of the text-conditioning pathway rather than scene-specific language understanding. Stronger controls such as shuffled captions, object-removed captions, captions from another image, or matched compute/parameter baselines would be needed to isolate the claimed mechanism.

The practical efficiency claim is incomplete. The paper argues for faster convergence and fewer diffusion steps, but the method also requires generating captions, including 740 GPU hours for training captions and an additional captioning model at test time when user descriptions are unavailable. The runtime and resource cost of caption generation are not incorporated into the efficiency comparison against Marigold.

The setup relies on LLaVA-generated captions for both training and evaluation, while the paper motivates human-provided language. There is no systematic evaluation with actual human descriptions, noisy human descriptions, terse commands, or domain-shifted language. This weakens claims about user intent and real-world controllable perception.

The small-region and controllability analyses are suggestive but not definitive. The small-area evaluation uses masks from MaskDINO and reports aggregate improvements, but it is unclear whether those masks correspond to objects actually mentioned in captions. The controllability examples are qualitative only, without a metric for caption-targeted improvement or degradation on unmentioned regions.

Some technical and presentation details reduce reproducibility and confidence. The paper says code will be released but does not provide it; several implementation choices are under-specified, such as exact depth encoding into the Stable Diffusion VAE, caption sampling details during training, and whether all baselines are evaluated with identical preprocessing. There are also formula/notation issues in the supplementary evaluation and normalization equations, including apparent inconsistencies in the affine normalization denominator and evaluation objective.

The originality is moderate rather than high. Conditioning a Stable Diffusion depth model on captions is a reasonable and useful idea, but it is an incremental extension of Marigold-like repurposing of text-to-image diffusion models, and the paper's evidence does not yet establish a substantially new capability beyond small accuracy gains and plausible qualitative improvements.

strengths: The paper studies a relevant and potentially useful direction: injecting language conditioning into diffusion-based monocular depth estimation, with a simple extension of a Marigold-like Stable Diffusion depth pipeline.
The method is technically plausible and mostly straightforward: image latents and noisy depth latents condition the denoising U-Net, while CLIP text embeddings provide the language condition.

The manuscript reports zero-shot evaluation on several standard datasets (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet), includes comparisons to depth estimators trained at different scales, and provides ablations on denoising steps, prompt templates, and small-area performance.
Implementation details are relatively concrete, including datasets, training iterations, optimizer, batch size, schedulers, normalization, caption generation prompts, and caption generation cost.
weaknesses: The central claim that language priors improve depth is not convincingly isolated. The captions are generated from the same image by LLaVA rather than supplied independently by humans, so the method may mostly distill an additional vision-language model's image interpretation back into the depth estimator. The paper does not separate language prior from extra test-time image analysis, nor evaluate real human descriptions.

The empirical gains over the most relevant baseline are small. Against the authors' reimplemented Marigold at 30k iterations, PriorDiffusion improves NYUv2 δ1 from 95.7 to 96.0 and KITTI from 89.7 to 90.3, with similarly modest AbsRel changes. These gains are useful but not strong enough to support the broad claims about resolving ambiguity, visual nuisance, and controllable perception.

The comparison protocol is somewhat fragile. The paper reports official Marigold numbers, reimplemented Marigold numbers, and PriorDiffusion numbers, but the reimplementation underperforms official Marigold on some datasets and exceeds it on others. This makes it hard to attribute improvements to language conditioning rather than training details, implementation differences, or checkpoint selection.

The claimed state-of-the-art performance is overstated. Depth Anything / Depth Anything v2 substantially outperform PriorDiffusion on NYUv2, KITTI, and ScanNet in Table 1, so the paper should frame the result as competitive among small-training-set diffusion methods rather than SOTA broadly.

The controllability evidence is mainly qualitative. Figures showing improved regions after adding text are interesting, but there is no rigorous evaluation that the model improves specifically on mentioned objects, handles contradictory descriptions robustly, or avoids hallucinating geometry from incorrect captions. The small-area evaluation uses MaskDINO masks but does not verify that those masks correspond to objects named in the text.

The efficiency claim is incomplete. The method may need LLaVA caption generation at inference when user captions are unavailable, and the appendix reports 3.6 seconds per caption plus large offline captioning cost. The reported faster denoising does not account for this language-generation overhead, which weakens the practical speed argument.

The ablations do not rule out simpler explanations. Template prompts and even blank or generic text inputs are close to the full method, suggesting that the benefit may come from training regularization or altered conditioning rather than image-specific language priors. A stronger control would train with random, shuffled, or generic captions under the same architecture and schedule.

The paper contains presentation and technical clarity issues: some equations and text are imprecise, there are repeated or malformed prompt descriptions, and the method description does not fully specify architectural changes such as how the Stable Diffusion U-Net input channels are adapted and initialized. These are fixable, but they affect reproducibility and confidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: improving zero-shot affine-invariant monocular depth estimation by exploiting text conditioning already present in pretrained text-to-image diffusion backbones. The idea is natural but useful, especially for small, ambiguous, occluded, or low-contrast regions where language can supply object identity and layout cues.

The method is technically plausible and cleanly integrated into an established diffusion-depth pipeline: Stable Diffusion v2 is adapted similarly to Marigold, with the depth latent, image latent, timestep, and CLIP text embedding used for denoising. This makes the contribution easy to understand and likely implementable.

The empirical comparison is reasonably broad for this area. The paper evaluates zero-shot transfer from synthetic HyperSim and Virtual KITTI training to NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, and ScanNet, and compares against both large-data foundation depth models and similarly trained diffusion baselines.

The results support a positive case for acceptance within the comparable-data regime. PriorDiffusion improves over the authors' Marigold reimplementation on most reported metrics, e.g. at 30k iterations it reports NYUv2 96.0/5.9 vs 95.7/6.1, KITTI 90.3/10.4 vs 89.7/10.7, ETH3D 95.8/6.5 vs 95.4/6.9, and ScanNet 94.9/6.7 vs 94.0/7.3.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond headline accuracy: convergence with fewer training iterations, inference performance under different denoising steps, small-region evaluation using MaskDINO masks, prompt/template ablations, and a failure case showing sensitivity to incorrect text.

Qualitative examples are well aligned with the paper's thesis, showing cases where described objects such as soap dispensers, signs, parked cars, shelves, or small transparent objects are better localized in depth than by the image-only baseline.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that improvements come from a learned language prior is only partially established. Since test captions are generated by LLaVA from the same image, the method uses an additional pretrained vision-language model at inference. The paper does not sufficiently disentangle gains from text semantics, LLaVA's visual recognition ability, extra compute/model capacity, or regularization from text conditioning during training.

The numerical gains over the strongest comparable baseline are consistent but modest. Several improvements over Marigold are around 0.1-0.6 absolute points in δ1 or AbsRel, and the method remains clearly behind very large-data models such as Depth Anything on NYUv2, KITTI, and ScanNet. The claim of state-of-the-art zero-shot performance is therefore too broad unless restricted to similarly sized training data or specific benchmarks.

The evaluation of human-provided or user-controllable text is mostly qualitative. The paper argues that users can guide perception by adding details, but there is no controlled quantitative study with human captions, deliberately varied captions, object-level annotations for mentioned vs unmentioned regions, or robustness analysis under realistic caption noise.

The inference setup may be impractical or unfairly specified. Generating captions on the fly with LLaVA adds substantial latency and compute, while using generated captions for every test image changes the comparison relative to image-only methods. The paper reports caption generation cost for training, but not full inference cost including captioning for deployment comparisons.

Some explanations are technically imprecise. For example, language is described as providing a good initialization of the diffusion trajectory, but the formulation still samples the same Gaussian latent and uses text as conditioning rather than initialization. This weakens the mechanistic interpretation of the faster denoising results.

The ablation evidence could be stronger. Template and blank-prompt results remain close to full text input, suggesting that part of the benefit may come from training with text conditioning or architectural differences rather than detailed language content. A stricter ablation with identical architecture, shuffled captions, mismatched captions, ground-truth object captions, and frozen/no-text variants would better support the claims.

Reproducibility is moderate but incomplete. The manuscript provides datasets, schedules, training iterations, batch size, prompts, and caption generation details, but the code is only promised for release, and some implementation details such as exact Marigold reimplementation differences, checkpoint selection, random seeds, ensemble settings across all baselines, and caption preprocessing are not fully specified.

Presentation has several polish issues, including grammatical errors, repeated template text, citation irregularities around LLaVA/ChatGPT, and some overclaiming in the abstract and conclusion. These are not fatal, but they make the manuscript feel less careful than the technical idea deserves.

strengths: The paper studies a clear and timely question: whether natural-language scene descriptions can improve diffusion-based monocular depth estimation by conditioning the denoising process on both image and text.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: the authors test the idea on three diffusion-based depth estimators or variants, train on synthetic HyperSim/Virtual KITTI, and report zero-shot results on NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet, and DIODE.

The reported results are mostly consistent: text conditioning improves the retrained baselines in many settings, with particularly clear gains for Marigold on DIODE, ScanNet, ETH3D AbsRel, and small segmented regions in NYUv2.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond the main table, including text-at-train vs text-at-test variants, fewer denoising steps, small-area evaluation, prompt ablations, number-of-caption ablations, and a failure case with incorrect text.

The implementation description is relatively detailed, including training schedules, datasets, caption generation models, and inference settings, which supports reproducibility if code and generated captions are released.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: the method appears to mainly reuse the existing Stable Diffusion text encoder/cross-attention pathway for depth estimation. This is a sensible adaptation, but the paper frames it as a broad finding rather than a clearly new algorithmic contribution.

The empirical gains are often small and sometimes mixed. For example, Marigold + Text improves over the retrained Marigold baseline by about 0.2 δ1 / 0.2 AbsRel on NYUv2 and 0.9 δ1 / 0.9 AbsRel on DIODE, while Lotus and E2E-FT gains are modest and some train-only or infer-only settings degrade performance.

Several claims about language resolving ambiguity and improving specified regions rely heavily on qualitative examples. The small-area evaluation is useful, but it uses automatic MaskDINO masks and does not verify that the evaluated regions are actually mentioned in the captions or semantically disambiguated by text.

The evidence does not fully isolate language semantics from generic text-conditioning regularization. Fixed template prompts and even generic inputs achieve comparable performance in Table 5, suggesting some improvements may come from training with the text pathway rather than meaningful scene descriptions.

The caption pipeline weakens the practical claim that language is available at no additional cost. LLaVA caption generation for Marigold is reported to require 740 GPU hours, and the paper does not analyze runtime, caption noise, or robustness at realistic deployment scale.

The comparison to original published baselines is somewhat hard to interpret because several retrained baselines underperform the reported original numbers, and the main improvements are often measured against these retrained versions rather than consistently stronger published checkpoints.
The paper lacks statistical uncertainty across seeds or caption samples, despite small performance differences. This makes it difficult to judge whether many of the reported improvements are robust.

The limitation discussion acknowledges misleading text but only with an anecdotal example. A systematic robustness study with incorrect, incomplete, generic, or adversarial captions would be important given that text quality is central to the method.

strengths: The paper studies a clear and potentially useful question: whether language descriptions can improve diffusion-based monocular depth estimation by reducing visual ambiguity. This is relevant for CV/robotics settings where text instructions or scene descriptions may be available.
The evaluation is broader than a single-model demonstration: the authors apply the idea to Marigold, Lotus-D/Lotus-G, and E2E-FT, and evaluate zero-shot on NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet, and DIODE.

The quantitative tables show some consistent gains when text is used in both training and inference, especially for Marigold, e.g. NYUv2 AbsRel 6.1 to 5.9, KITTI delta1 89.7 to 90.6, ETH3D AbsRel 6.9 to 6.5, and ScanNet AbsRel 7.3 to 6.7.

The paper includes useful ablations on train-only/infer-only text, prompt variants, denoising steps, fixed template prompts, and number of captions, plus a limitation example showing incorrect text can mislead the model.
The manuscript is generally understandable and provides implementation details for the three adapted baselines, including training schedules, caption generation models, and evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: The central empirical gains are mostly small and sometimes inconsistent. Text conditioning degrades or barely changes several settings: Marigold train-only is worse on NYUv2/KITTI/ScanNet, Lotus-D train-only is worse on most datasets, Lotus-G text variants are mixed, and E2E-FT improves some datasets but worsens DIODE. This weakens the broad claim that language generally improves diffusion-based depth estimation.

The test-time language descriptions are generated automatically from the same input image by strong VLMs, not provided independently by humans or task instructions. This makes the practical setting unclear: the system adds a second image-understanding model at inference time, with substantial extra compute and possible failure modes, but the paper does not report end-to-end runtime, captioning cost, or robustness to captioning errors beyond one qualitative example.

The novelty is limited. Stable-Diffusion-based depth models already contain text-conditioning machinery, and the method largely appears to reactivate or fine-tune existing CLIP text conditioning with generated captions. The contribution is closer to an empirical observation than a substantially new model or learning principle.

The evidence for the paper’s mechanistic explanation is not very strong. Claims that text reduces the 3D solution space, improves perception of specified regions, and provides geometric priors are mainly supported by qualitative examples and aggregate metrics; there is little causal analysis separating semantic guidance from regularization, caption style, extra parameters/conditioning, or VLM-derived scene cues.

The small-area analysis is suggestive but not fully convincing. It uses MaskDINO masks under area thresholds, but does not clearly establish that the evaluated masks correspond to objects actually mentioned in the captions, nor does it compare against equally detailed non-language controls or object/semantic masks without text.

The inference-speed claim is under-supported. The paper compares denoising-step convergence for Marigold with and without text, but does not include caption-generation latency or a fair accuracy/latency tradeoff against tuning the baseline sampler, using fewer steps with ensembling, or other accelerated diffusion-depth variants.

Reproducibility has gaps. Code and generated text data are promised only upon acceptance; prompts and training details are partly supplied, but generated captions, model checkpoints, seed variability, and exact splits/checkpoints are needed to reproduce small reported gains.

The paper compares to strong general depth methods in Table 1 but the proposed approach remains far behind Depth Anything/Depth Anything v2 on several datasets. That is not disqualifying by itself, but the manuscript’s claims should be framed more modestly as improving selected diffusion baselines rather than providing a broadly competitive depth estimator.

Presentation has signs of insufficient polish: the method is named Iris, but some figure captions refer to 'PriorDiffusion'; there are grammatical issues and repeated/duplicated prompt text in the supplement. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they reduce confidence in the care of the submission.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and timely question: whether the text-conditioning pathway already present in text-to-image diffusion backbones can improve diffusion-based monocular depth estimation. The idea is simple but useful, and the manuscript articulates a plausible mechanism through semantic, geometric, and spatial priors from language.

The evaluation is broader than a single-model demonstration. The authors test the strategy on Marigold, Lotus-D/Lotus-G, and E2E-FT, train on HyperSim and Virtual KITTI, and report zero-shot results on NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet, and DIODE. This breadth makes the positive trend more convincing than an isolated ablation.

The reported gains, while modest, are reasonably consistent when text is used in both training and inference. For example, Marigold improves from 95.7/6.1 to 95.9/5.9 on NYUv2, 89.7/10.7 to 90.6/10.4 on KITTI, and 94.0/7.3 to 94.9/6.7 on ScanNet; similar improvements appear for several Lotus and E2E-FT settings.

The paper includes targeted analyses beyond aggregate benchmark numbers, including small-region evaluation, prompt ablations, denoising-step comparisons, caption-count ablations, and qualitative examples showing improvements on described objects or ambiguous regions. These analyses support the claim that language helps most in semantically specific or visually subtle areas.
The limitation that incorrect text can misguide prediction is explicitly acknowledged and illustrated, which is important for a method whose inference depends on external descriptions.
weaknesses: The empirical improvements are often small and sometimes inconsistent. Text-only-at-training often hurts or gives negligible benefit, text-only-at-inference is mixed, and several metrics remain below stronger non-language baselines such as Depth Anything. The paper’s main claim is therefore best understood as a useful incremental conditioning strategy, not a large advance in depth estimation accuracy.

The novelty is moderate. The method largely reactivates or uses the existing CLIP/text-conditioning branch of Stable Diffusion based depth models, with standard diffusion training and inference. The main contribution is the systematic study and empirical finding rather than a technically new architecture or learning objective.

The evidence that language reduces the depth solution space through learned 3D priors is plausible but not directly demonstrated. Since the captions are generated from the same input image using VLMs, improvements may partly reflect additional image-derived semantic processing by a large external model rather than language priors alone. Experiments with human captions, deliberately controlled captions, object names only, spatial-relation-only captions, or captions from weaker/stronger VLMs would better isolate the mechanism.

The practical cost and deployment assumptions are underdeveloped. Generating captions for all training and test images requires an additional VLM and nontrivial compute, and real applications may not always have reliable human or VLM descriptions. The comparison does not clearly account for this extra inference-time model/cost relative to image-only baselines.

Robustness to caption errors is only lightly explored through a qualitative example. Since the method can be misled by wrong text, quantitative stress tests with missing objects, wrong spatial relations, hallucinated objects, and generic prompts would be important for safety-critical settings such as driving or embodied agents.

Reproducibility is reasonable in terms of implementation details and datasets, but the code and generated text data are only promised after acceptance. The exact caption-generation prompts differ across models and are only partly specified, which may make reproduction and fair comparison more difficult.

The presentation occasionally overstates conclusions relative to the evidence, especially around convergence acceleration, iterative refinement, and causal explanations of why text helps. These are interesting observations, but the support is mainly empirical and limited to selected settings.
